html:
The Mexico City earthquake struck on the morning of 19 September 1985. Its magnitude was 8.0, and it killed at least 5,000 people, with some estimates far higher.

The quake began off the Pacific coast, some 350 km away. Yet the worst damage was in Mexico City. The city stands on the soft clay of the old Lake Texcoco, where the Aztecs had built Tenochtitlan, and the soft ground shook like jelly. Hundreds of buildings collapsed, including hospitals and new apartment blocks.

The government of the ruling party, the PRI, was slow and confused, and at first turned down foreign help. Ordinary people dug through the rubble themselves. Volunteer rescue teams formed, and neighbourhood groups organised to demand new housing. Many historians see this as a turning point: Mexico's citizens learned to organise outside the party that had ruled since 1929.

Stricter building codes and an earthquake warning system followed. By an odd chance, another deadly quake struck central Mexico on the same date in 2017.
